protocol.baseline: one global popularity+recency page shown to every visitor
protocol.why_independent: Per-customer ground truth cannot be influenced by either arm — neither decides what that person actually bought in the test window. The cohort comparison lacked this property, which is why it favoured the bestseller page by construction.

the_finding: Personalisation does NOT lift projected revenue at this horizon: collaborative is -11.8% with a 95% CI of [-25.83, 3.96], which INCLUDES zero — a difference the data cannot distinguish from none. What it buys is REACH: 28.8% of the catalogue receives exposure against 0.09% for one bestseller page, a 325x increase, for no measurable revenue cost. For a retailer holding inventory, that is the trade: 325x the assortment working, at break-even. The revenue case for personalisation on this dataset is not proven; the ASSORTMENT case is, and it is the stronger argument because dead stock is a cost a bestseller page never addresses.
hypothesis_tested_and_rejected: This benchmark was built expecting per-visitor personalisation to beat the bestseller page, on the reasoning that the cohort comparison failed only because aggregate relevance IS popularity. It does not. Popularity beats every personalised arm on hit rate (0.0565 vs 0.0512 at k=10) while collaborative beats it on NDCG (0.0127 vs 0.0100) — collaborative finds slightly FEWER purchases but ranks the ones it finds better. Reported rather than reframed again: hunting for the comparison that produces the wanted answer is how an evaluation stops being one.
limitation: PROJECTED, not measured. Purchases, not impressions: a slot earns only where the customer bought that article, so both arms are understated and the LEVEL is not meaningful — the DIFFERENCE is. Position decay is declared, not fitted, because position bias is unobservable in this dataset.
